title:
Ovarian teratoma associated Anti-N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor encephalitis: a difficult
diagnosis with a favorable prognosis
case_prompt:
A 22-year-old woman with no significant medical history was brought to the emergency department after an acute deterioration in mental status. Over the preceding three weeks she developed mood swings, anxiety, depression, and progressive bradykinesia. On the day of admission she was found agitated and delirious, with a suicide attempt by jumping from a moving car. 

On arrival she was involuntarily held by psychiatry for altered mental status, uncooperativeness, agitation, and impulsive aggressive behavior. Initial noncontrast head CT and MRI of the brain showed no acute intracranial abnormalities. She was started on sodium valproate for presumed bipolar disorder with psychotic features, along with olanzapine and clonazepam. 

She was admitted to the medical ICU. Neurologic examination was limited by agitation and confusion, but cranial nerves II–XII appeared grossly intact. Her working diagnoses included encephalopathy (viral, fungal, bacterial, spirochetal, toxoplasmal, paraneoplastic antibody–mediated, and anti-NMDAR encephalitis), sepsis versus systemic inflammatory response syndrome from aspiration, and acute hypoxic respiratory failure. 

An extensive infectious, metabolic, autoimmune, and neurologic workup was initiated. Initial laboratory panels returned negative. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed a white blood cell count of 14.4/mm3 with lymphocytic pleocytosis; protein and glucose levels were normal. Empiric acyclovir was started pending herpes simplex virus (HSV) testing; preliminary HSV-1 and HSV-2 PCR results were negative.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Consideration of a primary psychiatric disorder was challenged because “the majority of these patients ... are misdiagnosed with new-onset psychiatric disorders and are started on anti-psychotics.”  
2. Common infectious causes of encephalitis were less likely since “initial panels have returned negative.”  
3. HSV encephalitis was ruled out as “the preliminary HSV type 1 and type 2 PCR results were negative; ... it was discontinued as soon as her final HSV type 1 and type 2 PCR report also came back negative.”  
4. Sepsis or SIRS from aspiration was considered given acute hypoxic respiratory failure but lacked supportive laboratory evidence.  
5. Paraneoplastic or autoimmune encephalitis remained on the differential as per the working diagnosis: “encephalopathy (including viral, fungal, bacterial, spirochetal, toxoplasmal, paraneoplastic antibodies, anti-NMDAR encephalitis).”
